# The Country of Night

There used to be a country that no longer exists. Its borders were the edge of the firelight and the first gray suggestion of dawn. Its citizens were everyone, because everyone had to live there. They didn't visit it. They inhabited it, the way fish inhabit water, for half of every year and most of every day, depending on the season. We have largely forgotten this country. We sealed its borders with electricity, and now we live in a continuous afternoon that stretches from one end of our lives to the other.

I want to write about that lost country — the night as it actually was, when darkness was not a vibe or a metaphor but a physical fact with weight and consequence — and about what happened to us, and to our minds, when we left it.

## The Price of Light

Start with a number that is hard to feel in your bones: for most of human history, light after sundown was staggeringly expensive. A candle burning in medieval England cost roughly the equivalent of a day's wages to run through the evening. Not a week. A single evening. A peasant family might own one tallow candle, made from rendered animal fat, that guttered and smoked and smelled like a slaughterhouse, and they would light it only for brief, necessary tasks — finding the chamber pot, checking a crying child, waiting up for someone who was late. Wood fires gave some light, but a fire is not a lamp; it pools in one room, it demands feeding, it fills the house with smoke. Oil lamps existed, whale oil later, but oil was money.

What this meant, in practice, was that when the sun went down, most people went with it. Not immediately — there were animals to see to, supper to eat, stories to tell in the communal glow of the hearth — but there was no such thing as an evening of reading, no late-night work session, no third episode. The day ended because the day had a shape, and the shape was the sky. In winter, this meant fifteen, sixteen hours of darkness. People went to bed at what we would now consider the late afternoon or early evening, and they stayed there a long time.

And here is where the country of night becomes strange, because they did not simply sleep straight through it.

## The Watch

The historian Roger Ekirch spent years digging through court records, diaries, letters, medical texts, and folklore from the pre-industrial world, and he found something that modern sleep science had entirely missed: for centuries, across cultures, people slept in two shifts. They went to bed a few hours after dusk, slept deeply for three or four hours, and then woke up. Not fitfully, not as a disorder — woke up calmly, into a distinctive interval of quiet wakefulness that they called by various names: the watch, the night waking, *dorveille* in French, a word that sits beautifully between sleep and waking. Then, after an hour or two of this, they fell asleep again until dawn.

This was not a folk quirk. It appears in the Bible, in Homer, in medical treatises, in a fifteenth-century Italian devotionary that prescribed specific prayers for the hour between sleeps, in diaries from the 1600s where people mention "first sleep" and "second sleep" the way we mention breakfast and lunch — as unremarkable structure. When researchers in the 1990s exposed volunteers to fourteen hours of darkness a night for a month, simulating winter in a pre-electric world, the two-sleep pattern emerged in the laboratory within weeks. It appears to be something the human body does when the lights go out for real. We didn't discover a new disorder when we started waking at 3 a.m. We may have rediscovered an old room in our own houses.

What did people do with that hour? Ekirch's sources are intimate on this point. They prayed. They reflected on dreams, which were considered more meaningful then — the interval between sleeps was thought to be when dreams were most legible, still warm from the other side. They talked. A husband and wife lying in the dark had a protected hour for conversation and, not incidentally, for sex, which the medical texts of the period actually recommended for this window, when the day's labor was done and the mind was soft. They smoked. They visited — in some villages, the night waking was mildly social, a neighbor stepping over in the dark to share news by the banked fire. And they simply lay there, in a state of consciousness that we now barely have a name for, half-dissolved, unhurried, with no electric ghost in the corner insisting that they should be doing something.

I find this almost unbearably poignant. We have pathologized the night waking, medicated it, and designed our whole relationship with darkness around the assumption that sleep is a single solid block, an eight-hour delivery we either receive in full or have failed at. The people of the lost country had a different arrangement with the night: they entered it, surfaced in the middle, kept company with themselves, and sank again. The night was not a void to be slept through as quickly as possible. It was a place with rooms.

## Night as Territory

And it was a place with occupants. This is the part that is easy to mock from our side of the electric line and hard to understand if you take it seriously.

When darkness is total, when the only light is a fire's ember and the wind is doing something in the thatch, the world does not feel empty. The pre-electric night was saturated with presence — souls of the dead, fairies, witches, angels, the dead again, always the dead, who were not as firmly elsewhere as we now keep them. Church bells marked the hours partly to assert, through the blackout, that the human order still existed. People laid out funeral bread, turned mirrors to the wall, avoided crossroads, whispered. A huge portion of the folklore that we now shelve as charming superstition was, in its original setting, a practical cartography of the dark. These were the maps people carried into a country that swallowed the body's primary sense.

This is not to say they were simply terrified. Fear was one register of a much richer relationship. Night was also when the poor could gather firewood or poach a rabbit without being seen; when lovers could meet; when the enslaved, in the American South, held their own gatherings in the woods, building what historians have called the invisible church, a whole spiritual life conducted in the hours the master could not easily police. Night was concealment, and concealment is freedom's crude first form. It was also the time of dreams, which carried, for most of human history, more ontological authority than they do now. The soul was thought to travel. The dead visited. The night was not the absence of the day's world. It was another world, adjacent, thinner-walled.

Above all of it, the sky. I want to dwell here for a second, because we have lost something in this domain so completely that most people reading this have never seen it. In the pre-electric night, the Milky Way was not a photograph or a name. It was a visible river of light overhead, bright enough, according to many accounts, to cast a faint shadow on clear nights. The stars were infrastructure. Sailors ran by them, farmers timed planting by them, travelers judged the hour by the turn of the Great Bear. Every culture on Earth projected its stories onto those stars and used those stories as calendars, ethics lessons, and navigation. The night sky was the oldest human screen, and it showed not content chosen for us but the actual universe, in an image of such scale that philosophers from Kant onward have treated the starry heavens as one of the two things that reliably produce the feeling of the sublime — the other being the moral law, which is a different essay.

Then we turned the night on, and the stars went out.

## The Conquest of Darkness

The conquest happened in stages, each one narrowing the night. Tallow gave way to beeswax, then to whale oil, then to kerosene. Gaslight arrived in the early nineteenth century and did something unprecedented: it let cities stay awake. The gaslit streets of London and Paris became famous, theatrical, slightly disreputable — night life was invented, in the sense of a public life that happens after dark for its own sake, among strangers, under artificial suns. Night shifts appeared. The distinction between day and night began its long career of blurring.

Then Edison, and the incandescent bulb, and the grid, and the twentieth century's project of total illumination. It is worth being honest that this was, in many ways, a triumph. Electric light reduced fires, extended the school day, made streets safer for many people, powered the hospitals, and gave millions of workers evening hours that belonged to them — hours for reading, for education, for the modern idea of a private life. I am not writing a pastoral lament. Artificial light is one of the genuine goods of the modern world, and anyone romanticizing darkness should have to spend a winter in a house that goes black at 4:30 p.m. with a sick child and no lamp.

But conquest has costs that don't show up on the victory monument. We did not merely extend the day. We abolished the night as an environment and replaced it with something that looks like night from inside a lit room but is, from outside and above, a pale amber dome hanging over every city on Earth. Fully a third of humanity now lives under skies too bright to see the Milky Way. For most people in the developed world, the stars have become a rumor, a thing you visit on vacation in a designated Dark Sky Reserve, like a national park for a sense that used to be free.

And our bodies noticed. The human circadian system is not a lifestyle preference. It is a deep architecture, tuned across millions of years to a bright blue morning, a golden late afternoon, and a darkness that means darkness — no blue-white rectangles held at close range, no streetlight leaking through curtains, no 2 a.m. scroll. Light at night suppresses melatonin, shifts the clock, fragments the architecture of sleep. Rates of insomnia have climbed in lockstep, more or less, with the electrification of the evening. We wake at 3 a.m. and, instead of resting in the old watch, we reach for the phone, which floods the eyes with noon-colored light and tells the brainstem that the day has begun. Then we wonder why we feel haunted.

## The 3 A.M. Mind

Because there is something at 3 a.m. — anyone who has been awake then knows it — and I do not think it is merely malfunction.

There is a particular consciousness that visits in the small hours, when the world's demands have gone quiet and the self is left alone with its inventory. It is not daytime thinking, that upright, purposeful, list-making mode. It is not dreaming. It is a third thing: slower, more permeable, with the volume turned down on the future and the volume turned up on everything unsaid. Worries that look small by daylight look structural at 3 a.m., and truths that look structural by daylight look small. Neither assessment is the true one. The 3 a.m. mind is a lens with an unusual curvature, and the mistake — ours, especially — is to believe whichever verdict it delivers and then, in the morning, either obey the despair or forget the insight.

The people of the lost country had a protocol for this state. They expected it. They gave it prayers, and a name, and a place in the architecture of the night, and then they went back to sleep. We have no protocol. We have a phone, a ceiling, and a growing sense that we are broken. Much of what we call insomnia, I suspect, is not a broken sleep system but an unlit room we no longer know how to sit in. The watch still comes. We just don't know what it is for, so we fill it with light and alarm, and then we cannot return to the second sleep, and we emerge at dawn feeling as if we've been beaten.

There is older knowledge about this, if you go looking. The mystics had it — the "dark night of the soul" is not a metaphor invented for poetry anthologies; it is a description of a real state that certain minds fall into when the usual light is withdrawn, and the tradition's counsel is not to fix it by 7 a.m. but to stay in it and let it work. The poets had it. Almost every contemplative tradition on Earth treats darkness, silence, and night as technologies of the interior, conditions under which the self can be seen without the day's makeup. The desert monastics went into actual darkness to find out what remained. What remained, they said, was the truth about themselves, and God, and not much else, and that this was the beginning of freedom.

I am not going to prescribe a desert. But I will say this: a mind that never meets genuine darkness is a mind that never gets off-stage. There is no interval, no holding pattern, no place where the performance can be put down. Light is attention, and our attention is now fully employed. Darkness is the withdrawal of attention from the world, and there used to be a whole culture built around doing that well — the two sleeps, the watch, the prayers for the hour between, the assumption that you would surface in the middle of the night and be a soul for a while before being a worker again.

## What the Dark Still Does

Go out, some clear night, somewhere the streetlights fail, and stand still for twenty minutes. That is roughly how long full night vision takes to develop, the pupils widening, the retina shifting over to its more sensitive rods. For the first several minutes you will be nearly blind, and this is the part modern people cannot tolerate — the blindness, the dependency, the loss of control. Stick it out. The world reassembles itself in silver. Trees that were black masses acquire leaves. The sky, if the sky is right, does the thing it does, the thing that has caused every culture that ever saw it to invent gods.

What you will feel, if you stay, is hard to say without slipping into the very language of the sublime that I said I'd be careful with. But something does happen. Scale happens. The human project, so total from inside a lit room, becomes a small lit room, and the night becomes what it always was: the default condition of the universe, the vast cold background against which our brief bright experiment is being run. Kant thought this feeling was morally useful, that it calibrated the self to something larger than the self. The people of the lost country got this calibration every clear night of their lives, free, along with their stories and their second sleep.

I don't want the night back the way it was. I like vaccines and reading lamps and not dying of exposure. But I want a border crossing. I want the night to be a country again, even if only occasionally, a place you enter and are changed by, rather than a dim settings menu you never open. Practically, this means darker bedrooms, fewer screens in the last hour, warm light after sundown, curtains that actually close, and — when it can be managed — a walk into real darkness a few times a year, no flashlight unless needed, long enough for the eyes to give up on the day. It might mean, if you wake at 3, not reaching for the phone. Lying in the dark. Letting the watch be what it was: an interval between two sleeps, a room in the old house, a time for thinking without the day's bright pressure, and then a sinking back down.

The country of night is not gone. It was never gone. It is right there, on the other side of the light switch, the oldest country, the one we all came from, still keeping its two-sleep customs, its stars, its strange 3 a.m. court where the self sits in session. We stopped going. That is all. And the door is not locked. It is just, for the first time in the entire history of the species, up to us whether we open it.

That is a strange inheritance. We are the first people who have to choose the dark. Everyone before us was carried into it by the sun's leaving, ready or not. We can stay in the light indefinitely, and many of us do, and we pay for it in sleep and stars and a certain flatness of soul that we mostly blame on other things. Or we can, now and then, do the old thing on purpose: put out the light, let the eyes widen, let the mind widen with them, and visit the country that raised us, where the dead used to be near, the watch used to be kept, and the sky was a roof over everything, and nobody had to be told to look up.
